sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities finished mixed-to-lower as an AI-driven technology wobble, a sharp rise in oil and a looming Fed decision dominated sentiment. MSCI World eased roughly **0.7%** to **4,874.68**, with MSCI Developed Markets broadly similar and MSCI Emerging Markets near **1,578**, weighed down by China. The S&P 500 slipped **0.5%** to **7,623.68** and the Nasdaq fell **0.7%** to **25,955.34** on a second straight weekly loss, with the mega-cap MAG7 cohort again leading the decline, while the Dow bucked the trend, up **0.4%** to **52,215.16**. In Europe the Euro Stoxx 50 dropped **2.2%** to about **6,068**. Across APAC, Japan's Nikkei 225 closed Friday near **62,693**, China's CSI 300 slid into bear-market territory around **4,105** and Hong Kong's Hang Seng ended near **23,093**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities were choppy and finished mixed as AI-valuation jitters, a surge in oil and a looming FOMC decision offset a busy run of Q3 earnings. The S&P 500 slipped **0.5%** to **7,623.68** and the Nasdaq Composite fell **0.7%** to **25,955.34**, its second consecutive weekly loss, while the Dow added **0.4%** to **52,215.16** for a third straight weekly gain as defensive and value names outperformed.

Leadership was narrow and defensive. Energy was the standout as Brent crude jumped, whereas technology and communication services lagged, each shedding around **3%** on Friday, and the mega-cap MAG7 cohort stayed under pressure. American Express fell more than **3%** after announcing job cuts, underscoring a cautious tone beneath the headline indices.

Macro and policy framed the week. September CPI had reaccelerated to **3.7%** y/y, and with the Fed having lifted rates to **3.75–4.00%** in September, attention turned to the 28 October FOMC meeting and the mega-cap earnings slate, including Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, due the following week.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities posted their steepest weekly loss since early September. The pan-regional STOXX Europe 600 fell about **1.4%** to **635.77**, while the Euro Stoxx 50 dropped **2.2%** to roughly **6,068**, with Germany's DAX near **25,236**, France's CAC 40 around **7,759** and the UK's FTSE 100 about **10,687**.

French budget turmoil, a climbing oil price and spillover from the US technology sell-off drove the retreat. Luxury weighed heavily after Kering slumped on soft Gucci sales, defence names fell sharply following Safran's results, and the euro-area composite PMI slowed to **51.9** from **53.1**, denting the growth backdrop.

Dispersion was pronounced, with energy supported by firmer crude while rate-sensitive and globally exposed sectors lagged. With the ECB decision due the following week, investors stayed defensive into Friday's close amid sticky inflation and fragile risk appetite.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian equities were pressured by the global technology sell-off, led lower by Japan, where the Nikkei 225 closed Friday near **62,693** after a volatile week as a sharp drop in US semiconductors — the SOX fell **6.7%** on Thursday — reverberated across chip-related names.

Chinese markets were weaker still, with the CSI 300 sliding into bear-market territory, more than **20%** below its peak, before a **1.7%** Friday bounce to around **4,105** pared losses after a prolonged losing streak. Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose **0.7%** on Friday to about **23,093**, while South Korea's Kospi steadied at **5,550.30** after an intraday slide of more than **4%**.

Policy signals added to the cross-currents. The BoJ, having raised its policy rate to **1.25%** in September, loomed over markets ahead of its 30 October meeting, while concerns over AI valuations and Chinese tech competition kept higher-beta names volatile.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar stayed firm, extending a broad rally built on the Fed's return to tightening, elevated US yields and renewed safe-haven demand. The euro slipped towards a one-year low, with EUR/USD around **1.1161–1.1193**, as French fiscal strains and slowing eurozone activity capped the single currency.

The yen found some footing, supported by falling sovereign yields outside Japan and a hawkish repricing of BoJ expectations after September's hike to **1.25%**, though the still-wide US–Japan rate differential limited the recovery. Sterling traded a steady **1.31–1.33** range against the dollar.

Rate differentials and risk sentiment remained the key drivers, with the ECB and BoJ decisions the following week firmly in focus. Late-week risk aversion lent havens modest support, while higher-beta emerging-market currencies came under pressure from firmer oil and the equity wobble.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Oil dominated the complex. Brent crude settled Friday at **$116.72**, up **3.1%** on the day and roughly **5%** on the week for a third straight weekly advance and its highest settlement since April, after reported Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia revived supply-risk premia; WTI traded near **$103.27**.

Precious and base metals were more mixed. Gold eased to about **$3,994** amid profit-taking after its strong run, even as falling real yields offered a cushion, while copper held firm near **$6.48** per pound, up around **1.8%**, supported by electrification and structural demand themes.

The oil surge carried clear cross-asset implications, reviving inflation concerns, pressuring equities and complicating the outlook for rate cuts. The energy-led gains underpinned the broader commodity complex even as growth worries and a firm dollar tempered enthusiasm elsewhere.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign bonds rallied as investors fled risk assets. The 10-year UST ended the week at **5.00%** and the 2-year at **4.69%**, leaving the 2s10s spread near **31bp**, after a dramatic mid-week move on Thursday when the 10-year dropped about **19bp** — its largest one-day fall in roughly three and a half years — to near **4.95%** and the 2-year fell close to **19bp**.

The policy backdrop stayed hawkish by recent standards. With the Fed funds target at **3.75–4.00%** following September's hike, markets priced only a small chance of an October move ahead of the 28 October FOMC, but kept the odds of a further hike by year-end elevated, with surging oil seen limiting room to ease.

Credit tone softened alongside the equity de-risking, as weakness in technology and communications sapped risk appetite; HY spreads came under modest pressure while IG proved more resilient, aided by the flight-to-quality bid in core government bonds.
